balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

ntiMix.title: Net trading income mix
ntiMix.content:
Net Trading Income (NTI) is the bid-ask spread Flow Traders captures market making, split into Traditional (ETFs, fixed income, FX, commodities) and Digital Assets (crypto ETPs and related instruments).

For Flow Traders: Traditional NTI is the primary growth engine (+26% YTD26) while Digital Assets NTI is down 46% YoY YTD26 following the 10 October 2025 crypto liquidation event, even though it grew 21% QoQ in 3Q26. The mix shift matters more than the consolidated total.

What to watch:

  • Traditional NTI growth continuing to offset a slower Digital Assets recovery
  • Whether Digital Assets NTI re-accelerates as crypto markets normalise
  • Both legs are volatility-dependent, not recurring -- a single weak quarter (3Q26) can swing the total 40%+

tradingCapital.title: Trading capital and return on trading capital
tradingCapital.content:
Trading Capital is the balance sheet capital deployed to take on inventory risk while market making. Return on Trading Capital (RoTC) is NTI (or EBITDA, depending on the period) annualised against average trading capital deployed -- the key capital-efficiency metric for a market maker.

For Flow Traders: the Horizon 2030 plan (Capital Markets Day, June 2026) targets RoTC >50% by 2030. Trading Capital grew 34% YoY to €1,137m by end-3Q26, but RoTC fell to just 30% in 3Q26 (from 53% in 2Q26 and 37% in 3Q25) -- direct evidence the larger capital base is a drag on returns, not just embedded upside, when volatility is low. YTD26 RoTC of 47% is already below both YTD25's 59% and the long-term 50% ambition.

What to watch:

  • RoTC trending back toward or away from the 50% ambition as the capital base keeps growing
  • Trading Capital growth outpacing NTI growth (capital deployed without commensurate return)
  • The $200m private credit facility (secured Oct-2025) funding further expansion regardless of near-term RoTC

averageVix.title: Average VIX vs net trading income
averageVix.content:
The VIX (CBOE Volatility Index) is the standard proxy for market volatility. Flow Traders' revenue is transactional and volatility/volume-dependent rather than recurring -- wider bid-ask spreads and heavier flow in turbulent markets translate directly into higher NTI.

For Flow Traders: the 3Q26 NTI collapse (-43% QoQ to €84.5m) coincided with subdued volatility and a 6% QoQ drop in global ETF value traded, while episodic geopolitical volatility spikes (and the subsequent de-escalation, e.g. the mid-2026 Middle East ceasefire) have moved NTI in both directions. Revenue tracks volatility, not a secular growth curve.

What to watch:

  • NTI direction following VIX regime changes with a short lag
  • Low-volatility stretches compressing margins even as Trading Capital keeps growing
  • Don't extrapolate a single volatile (or quiet) quarter into a trend

etpValueTraded.title: ETP value traded: Flow vs the market
etpValueTraded.content:
Flow ETP value traded is the euro value of ETPs Flow Traders itself executed; Flow total value traded adds non-ETP instruments (fixed income, FX, commodities); Market ETP value traded is the entire market's ETP volume, roughly two orders of magnitude larger. The ratio of the first to the third is Flow's implied market share.

For Flow Traders: the business holds roughly a quarter of the EMEA ETF market but only a low-single-digit global share, as Citadel Securities and Jane Street dominate U.S. mega-cap ETFs. Flow increasingly pursues large-block RFQ/OTC flow in the Americas rather than head-to-head on-exchange competition there.

What to watch:

  • Flow's ETP volume growing faster or slower than the total market (share gain/loss)
  • Market volume swings dominate both lines in volatile quarters -- a volume spike is not necessarily share gain
  • APAC and China (launched H2 2025) as the next volume-growth lever

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Flow Traders Ltd.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
